findings.title: Tenant national ID numbers are stored in plaintext
findings.evidence: The column is declared `national_id text` in the `tenants` table with no encryption. The write path passes the value through untouched: `national_id: blankToNull(fields.national_id) || blankToNull(fields.id_number)` (app/api/tenants/route.ts:65) and `update.national_id = blankToNull(fields.national_id) || blankToNull(fields.id_number)` (app/api/tenants/[id]/route.ts:57). The value is read back in clear text by GET /api/tenants (app/api/tenants/route.ts:29-40) and copied verbatim into every backup snapshot (lib/backup.ts:181-203).
findings.impact: A Kenyan national ID is a state-issued identity-document number and the highest-value field in the schema: it is sufficient for identity fraud and is special-category-adjacent personal data under the Data Protection Act 2019. Every path that can read the table — a leaked DATABASE_URL, a Neon branch share, a read-only role, the `backups.payload` jsonb snapshot, or the CSV export — yields it in clear text for every customer of the platform. There is no field-level control at all today.
findings.fix: Encrypt `tenants.national_id` with AES-256-GCM in randomised mode using the `v1:<iv>:<tag>:<ct>` envelope and the key registry in audit/design/encryption-design.md sections 3-4. No blind index is required: national IDs are displayed, never searched. Add a new `tenants.national_id_enc` column rather than repurposing `national_id`, so the read path can migrate with a decrypt-then-migrate fallback, and backfill with scripts/backfill-encryption.ts (design section 9).
findings.fix_notes: The encryption core (lib/crypto/field-encryption.ts, AES-256-GCM with a versioned envelope) and the per-column plan (lib/crypto/pii-columns.ts) are implemented and tested — 53 assertions in lib/crypto/field-encryption.test.ts, plus an independent probe. national_id is in the plan. NOT YET CLOSED: the live rows are still plaintext. The read/write paths have to be wired (audit/deliverable-encryption-core.md section 5) and the backfill has to run. See HARDENING_RUNBOOK.md section 4.

findings.title: Tenant phone numbers are stored in plaintext and matched by an unscoped public query
findings.evidence: `select id from public.tenants where phone = ${phone} or phone like ${"%" + phone.slice(-9)} limit 1` runs on the public, unauthenticated M-Pesa C2B validation endpoint (app/api/mpesa/c2b/validation/route.ts:32-35) and filters by no tenant at all — it scans every landlord's tenants on the platform. The `tenants.phone` column is plain `text` (db/migrations/001-core.sql:83) and is written verbatim at app/api/mpesa/stkpush/route.ts:69.
findings.impact: The phone number of every tenant on the platform is plaintext and cross-queryable by an unauthenticated caller; the endpoint returns only a boolean, but it is an oracle over the whole tenant base. The unindexed `LIKE '%…'` scan also leaks table cardinality and row position through latency. For the implementation track: this query breaks the moment `phone` is encrypted, so the design must ship a blind index or the endpoint silently stops matching tenants.
findings.fix: Encrypt `tenants.phone` (randomised) and add `tenants.phone_bidx` — HMAC-SHA256 over the normalised E.164 number using a separate blind-index key (design section 5). Rewrite the lookup as `where phone_bidx = ${blindIndex(normalizePhone(msisdn))} and user_id = ${ownerUserId}`; the paybill owner is already resolvable via resolveOwnerByShortCode (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:98-117), which also removes the cross-tenant scan.
findings.fix_notes: Blind indexes are implemented (HMAC-SHA256 with a separate key) and the columns are added by db/migrations/005-encryption.sql. NOT YET CLOSED: the unscoped public phone lookup in app/api/mpesa/c2b/validation/route.ts still compares plaintext phone, and the call sites are not wired. The exact replacement query is in the integration checklist.

findings.title: M-Pesa payer identity (MSISDN and legal name) is stored in plaintext outside any tenant FK
findings.evidence: `c2b_transactions` declares `msisdn text`, `first_name text`, `middle_name text`, `last_name text` with no foreign key to `tenants` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:90-116). `mpesa_transactions.phone text not null` (db/migrations/002-support.sql:295) holds the same MSISDN. Both are written straight off the Daraja callback: `raw = ${JSON.stringify(body)}` (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:172) and `phone: normalized` (app/api/mpesa/stkpush/route.ts:69).
findings.impact: The payer's phone number and legal name are persisted in clear text in tables that are not bound to a tenant record. When a landlord deletes a tenant these rows survive untouched, so offboarding leaves the payer's identity behind forever — directly contradicting the deletion promise on the privacy page. PropDesk is also holding personal data about a third party (the payer) with no retention basis.
findings.fix: Encrypt `mpesa_transactions.phone`, `c2b_transactions.msisdn` and the three name columns in randomised mode (design section 6). On tenant offboarding, redact rather than orphan these values — see design section 9 and CRYPTO-013.
findings.fix_notes: msisdn, first_name, middle_name and last_name on c2b_transactions are in the per-column plan and the blind-index migration. NOT YET CLOSED: the call sites are not wired and the backfill has not run.

findings.title: Raw Daraja payloads are persisted as plaintext jsonb, duplicating the PII the column plan would protect
findings.evidence: `raw_callback: body` (app/api/mpesa/callback/route.ts:76) and `raw = ${JSON.stringify(body)}` (app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:174) write the entire Daraja payload, which contains CallbackMetadata.PhoneNumber, MpesaReceiptNumber, FirstName/LastName and the account reference. The columns are `raw_response jsonb` and `raw_callback jsonb` (db/migrations/002-support.sql:305-306) and `raw jsonb` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:114).
findings.impact: Any encryption plan that covers `msisdn` but not `raw` is defeated: the same phone number and payer name sit in clear text one column over. A `select *` on either table — which every incident-response dump does — leaks the full PII set regardless of the rest of the plan. This is the most likely way an implementation of the design is silently broken.
findings.fix: Replace the raw payload with a whitelisted subset (TransID, TransTime, TransAmount, BusinessShortCode, BillRefNumber, MpesaReceiptNumber, ResultCode) and drop the remainder before the insert; store the discarded fields nowhere. If the full payload must be retained for reconciliation disputes, encrypt the whole jsonb blob with the same envelope format (design section 3) instead.
findings.fix_notes: The raw Daraja payload is still persisted as plaintext jsonb. The integration checklist identifies the two write sites (c2b/confirmation and mpesa/callback).

findings.title: The `documents` storage bucket is PUBLIC, so the storage RLS policies do not protect identity documents
findings.evidence: `INSERT INTO storage.buckets (id, name, public) VALUES ('documents', 'documents', true)` (supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:326-328, repeated at supabase-setup/02-add-missing-columns.sql:65-67), with the comment at :353-355 claiming 'The bucket is public-readable so the app can render the URL directly ... Files are still scoped per-user via the path prefix (userId/...) enforced by the policies above.' The upload route returns a permanent public URL: `supabase.storage.from("documents").getPublicUrl(path)` (app/api/documents/upload/route.ts:48), stored in `documents.file_url` (db/migrations/001-core.sql:191).
findings.impact: A public Supabase bucket bypasses RLS entirely for reads, so the four storage.objects policies at supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:336-351 are inert for reads and the 'scoped per-user via the path prefix' comment is wrong. The bucket holds national ID scans, passports, lease agreements and identity documents. The URL is persisted in documents.file_url, returned by /api/export (app/api/export/route.ts:27) and /api/backup/csv/[table], and pasted into e-mail and WhatsApp by landlords. One leaked link is permanent, unauthenticated, unexpirable access to a tenant's identity document, with no access log. The `${userId}/…` prefix is a guessing barrier only, and userIds are UUIDs that appear in other URLs.
findings.fix: 1) `update storage.buckets set public = false where id = 'documents';` 2) Replace getPublicUrl with createSignedUrl(path, 300) at upload time plus a signed-URL read endpoint, and store the object path in documents.storage_path rather than a public URL. 3) Add a bucket policy allowing a signed-in user to read only objects under their own prefix, and perform uploads with the authenticated client rather than the service role.
findings.fix_notes: The documents bucket is created private and the storage policies are owner-scoped USING/WITH CHECK clauses, so they are finally meaningful for reads. Re-running the SQL flips an existing public bucket to private (ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET public = false). Every read goes through a 5-minute signed URL bound to the requesting owner. The live project still needs the bucket flipped by hand — runbook section 6.

findings.title: Property photos bypass the storage path policy and land in the same public bucket
findings.evidence: The object path is `property-photos/${userId}/${params.id}/${randomUUID()}.${ext}` (:57). The RLS policy expects the first path segment to be the user id — `auth.uid()::text = (storage.foldername(name))[1]` (supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:340-342) — so the policy would reject this upload. The route only succeeds because it upgrades to the service-role client (`createServiceClient(url, serviceKey, ...)` at :61-63), which bypasses RLS, and it then stores a permanent public URL: `getPublicUrl(path)` (:70) into `property_photos.file_url` (:96).
findings.impact: The ownership check the policy was written to perform is not performed at all — the service key writes anywhere — and the resulting URL is permanent and public. Property photos are the strongest physical-security signal in the dataset: a photo of the gate, water tank or compound plus properties.address identifies the landlord's home, and combined with the tenant list identifies the landlord's tenants.
findings.fix: Create a separate private bucket `property-photos` (public = false), change the path to `${userId}/${propertyId}/${uuid}.${ext}` so it satisfies the folder-prefix policy, upload with the authenticated client (drop the service-role branch at :61-63), and serve via short-lived signed URLs.
findings.fix_notes: Property photos are written to {userId}/property-photos/{propertyId}/{uuid}.{ext}, which satisfies the owner-prefix policy. The upload verifies the property belongs to the caller BEFORE uploading, sniffs the image magic bytes, and uses the user-scoped Supabase client instead of the service role. Reads return signed URLs.

findings.title: There is no application-layer encryption, no key material and no key registry
findings.lines: 36-42 (no lib/crypto/ exists anywhere in the repository)
findings.evidence: `getDb()` opens a Neon HTTP connection (`cachedSql = neon(url)`, lib/db/neon.ts:40) and every column in the data inventory is stored as plain text. There is no `lib/crypto/` module, no envelope format, no key id, no rotation support, and no reference to PROPDESK_ENCRYPTION_KEY anywhere in the repository.
findings.impact: The Neon connection string is the only control between an attacker and every landlord's tenant PII. A leaked DATABASE_URL (Vercel env var, a .env on a laptop, a Neon branch share, a sql.unsafe injection) yields plaintext national IDs, phone numbers and M-Pesa records for every customer. The published security page already tells the market the product is 'AES-256 at rest' (app/(marketing)/security/page.tsx:16) — a claim that is only true of the infrastructure provider's disk, not of the application's data. A single shared key is also a single point of compromise for the whole platform.
findings.fix: Implement lib/crypto/field-encryption.ts exactly as specified in audit/design/encryption-design.md section 3: AES-256-GCM via node:crypto, `v1:<iv>:<tag>:<ct>` envelope, key registry loaded from PROPDESK_ENCRYPTION_KEYS, and per-tenant data-encryption keys wrapped by a master key (design section 8) so a single key compromise is bounded. Then apply the per-column plan in design section 6.
findings.fix_notes: RESOLVED AS BUILT, NOT AS DEPLOYED. lib/crypto/field-encryption.ts implements AES-256-GCM with a 12-byte random IV per call, a versioned base64 envelope, a multi-key registry loaded from PROPDESK_ENCRYPTION_KEYS, key rotation via decryptFieldWithRotation(), and a fail-loudly path when the key is missing or the wrong length. 53 tests plus an independent probe. NOT YET CLOSED: no key is configured and no row is encrypted.

findings.title: CRON_SECRET is compared with a non-constant-time string comparison
findings.evidence: `const got = auth.replace(/^Bearer\s+/i, "").trim(); if (got !== secret) { return errorResponse("Forbidden: missing or invalid CRON_SECRET", 403) }`.
findings.impact: A non-constant-time string comparison short-circuits on the first differing byte, so response time varies with how many leading characters of the guess are correct; a remote attacker can recover the secret incrementally. Secondary issue in the same block: when CRON_SECRET is unset the endpoint is fully open — the unset case is only rejected in production (app/api/cron/run/route.ts:23-25) — and the route is a public POST.
findings.fix: Compare sha256(got) against sha256(expected) with crypto.timingSafeEqual over fixed 32-byte digests (no length oracle, no timingSafeEqual throw risk), and fail closed in all environments. Use the shared helper specified in design section 4.
findings.fix_notes: lib/api/secure-compare.ts timingSafeEqualString() is used by app/api/cron/run/route.ts.

findings.title: MIGRATION_SECRET is compared with `===` on three routes that can execute SQL against the live database
findings.evidence: `if (expected && got === expected) return null` in app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:49, app/api/migrations/reset/route.ts:44 and app/api/migrations/rollback/route.ts:35.
findings.impact: The same timing leak as CRYPTO-008, with a much larger blast radius: MIGRATION_SECRET authorises `await (sql as any).unsafe(sqlText)` at app/api/migrations/run/route.ts:117 — arbitrary SQL against the live production database — and app/api/migrations/rollback/route.ts:80 to run rollback SQL. A recovered secret is full database control, including the ability to read or exfiltrate every encrypted field.
findings.fix: Timing-safe digest comparison as in CRYPTO-008. Rotate the secret after the deployment window, and consider requiring an additional Vercel deployment-protection header on these three routes.
findings.fix_notes: lib/api/secure-compare.ts timingSafeEqualString() is used by app/api/migrations/run, /reset and /rollback. The fail-closed behaviour (503 when unset, 403 on mismatch) is unchanged.

findings.title: BACKUP_CRON_SECRET is compared with `===`, and the endpoint is unauthenticated when it is unset
findings.evidence: `if (!expected) { if (process.env.NODE_ENV === "production") { ...503... } return null // dev only }` (:28-36) and `return got === expected ? null : NextResponse.json({ error: "Forbidden" }, { status: 403 })` (:38).
findings.impact: In every non-production environment the endpoint is unauthenticated, and it is a bulk data-exfiltration primitive: it enumerates every user with auto_backup = true (app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:54) and writes a full plaintext snapshot of their data (app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:95-110). The comparison itself also leaks the secret.
findings.fix: Timing-safe digest comparison; require the secret unconditionally in every environment; and scope each invocation to a single explicit user_id instead of enumerating all users.
findings.fix_notes: lib/api/secure-compare.ts timingSafeEqualString() is used by app/api/backup/auto/route.ts. The endpoint still fails closed when the secret is unset.

findings.title: The M-Pesa callback secret check is timing-safe but leaks the secret's length and compares code units against bytes
findings.evidence: `if (!providedSecret || providedSecret.length !== callbackSecret.length || !timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(providedSecret), Buffer.from(callbackSecret))) { ... 403 ... }`.
findings.impact: This is the only secret comparison in the codebase that uses timingSafeEqual, and the equal-length guard is present and correct — good. Two residual issues: the guard compares UTF-16 code-unit counts (.length) while timingSafeEqual compares byte lengths, so the two quantities diverge for a secret containing a multi-byte character; and the guard is a length oracle, letting an attacker learn the exact secret length before guessing bytes. On a public endpoint this is free reconnaissance.
findings.fix: Hash both sides first and compare fixed-length digests: `timingSafeEqual(sha256(provided), sha256(expected))`. This removes the length oracle, the unicode/byte mismatch and the unequal-length throw hazard in one move. Apply the same helper to CRYPTO-008, CRYPTO-009 and CRYPTO-010.
findings.fix_notes: The M-Pesa callback secret comparison now goes through the shared constant-time helper and the length is not leaked separately.

findings.title: No account-deletion path exists, although the privacy policy and the help centre both promise one
findings.evidence: The privacy policy states: 'You can export, correct or delete your data at any time from Settings -> Data.' The help centre states: 'Yes - Settings -> Data -> Delete account. We delete within 30 days, except records we're legally required to keep.' The Settings -> Data tab renders only an 'Export Data' card with two download links (app/dashboard/settings/page.tsx:370, :411, :419) — there is no delete control anywhere in the application. There is no DELETE /api/account route, no auth.admin.deleteUser() call and no auth.users delete in app/api/** or lib/**; the only session-ending path is signOut (lib/actions.ts:109-117), which deletes nothing.
findings.impact: A provable, published false statement about the product's data-protection capability, repeated on two public pages. Every data-subject request PropDesk receives today is one it has advertised it can satisfy and cannot. Under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 a controller must honour a data subject's right to erasure, and under the DPA the processor must assist the customer within statutory timeframes. It is also the one claim a regulator or an aggrieved former landlord can verify in five minutes.
findings.fix: Implement DELETE /api/account per design section 9: wipe every user_id-scoped table (including the tables in lib/system.ts:22-42 that the current BACKUP_TABLES list omits), delete the user's Storage objects, delete the Supabase Auth user, write a non-identifying tombstone, and surface the 30-day promise in the settings UI. Until it ships, change the two pages to describe export and correction only.

findings.title: Tenant offboarding leaves the tenant's PII behind in tables with no cascade
findings.evidence: DELETE /api/tenants/[id] deletes the tenants row and nothing else. `documents.tenant_id` is `on delete set null` (db/migrations/001-core.sql:193), so the document row and its file_url survive. `c2b_transactions` has no FK to tenants at all and keeps msisdn, first_name, last_name and the full raw payload. `rent_payments.tenant_id` does cascade (db/migrations/001-core.sql:101), but `reconciliation_audit.matched_tenant_id` is `on delete set null` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:395) and its notes column carries the match commentary.
findings.impact: The action a landlord takes to remove a former tenant does not remove the tenant's identity document, their phone number, their payer's name and MSISDN, or their payment history from the database. Because c2b_transactions is not FK-bound, those rows are invisible to any per-tenant cleanup query. The result is unbounded retention of a natural person's data with no legitimate basis.
findings.fix: On tenant delete, run a redaction sweep over documents (row plus Storage object), c2b_transactions (MSISDN, names, raw), mpesa_transactions, notifications and reconciliation_audit for that tenant. Encrypted columns make this feasible: decrypt and replace with a fixed tombstone value, or null the column for that row. See design section 9.

findings.title: The backup subsystem is a permanent plaintext replica of every PII field, and restore writes plaintext back
findings.lines: 181-203 and 286-300 (also lib/storage.ts:26-57, app/api/backup/auto/route.ts:95-110, app/api/export/route.ts:20-29, lib/system.ts:22-42 and :132-152)
findings.evidence: exportBackup runs `select *` over 19 tables — including tenants, contacts, c2b_transactions, documents and reconciliation_audit — and returns the rows verbatim. The result is stored as plaintext JSON in `backups.payload` jsonb (lib/backup.ts:297) or uploaded verbatim to the `backups` Storage bucket with contentType application/json and no encryption (lib/storage.ts:34-40). sanitiseRow (lib/system.ts:145-152) strips only 11 credential-shaped column names (password, token, secret, api_key, ...); national_id, phone, email, msisdn and raw are not on that list, so all of them are copied into the backup. prune_old_backups (supabase-setup/12-auto-backup.sql:11-30) keeps the 50 most recent snapshots per user, so plaintext PII accumulates indefinitely. The payload is served back to the browser at app/api/backup/[id]/route.ts:21 and is the input to restore (app/api/backup/import/route.ts:53 -> lib/backup.ts:209-260), which writes rows straight back with `insert ... on conflict do update`.
findings.impact: The backup table and the backups bucket are functionally a second plaintext database containing national ID numbers, and they are the least protected part of the system: the backups bucket has no storage policy at all (only documents gets one, supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:331-351), the payload is downloadable by the account owner at any time, and a restore after encryption would write plaintext PII straight back into the encrypted columns. Any deletion flow that touches only the source tables leaves the backup copy intact, which is why the 'delete my data' promise in CRYPTO-012 is currently impossible to keep.
findings.fix: Encrypt the backup payload with a dedicated backup key before persisting or uploading and decrypt on download; add national_id, id_number, phone, msisdn and email to a PII-aware redaction list for the CSV/JSON export path; make restore decrypt-aware so it never writes plaintext into an encrypted column; and define explicit policies for the backups bucket. See design section 9.

findings.title: There is no record of who read or changed sensitive data
findings.lines: 1-327 (no audit table in this file; the only audit-shaped table is supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:389-408)
findings.evidence: The only audit table is `reconciliation_audit` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:389-400), which records payment matching decisions only. There is no table, middleware hook or wrapper that records 'user X read tenant Y's national ID', 'user X exported the tenants table' or 'user X downloaded an identity document'. lib/api/index.ts:55 and lib/api/with-db-auth.ts:106 log request failures to stdout and nothing else.
findings.impact: A landlord who suspects a former employee or a compromised session exported their tenants' national IDs has no way to detect it, prove it, or bound it: there is no access log, no download log and no export log. PropDesk cannot answer a data-subject access request ('who saw my ID number?'), cannot perform forensic investigation after a breach, and cannot meet the DPA's own promise of 'audit logging' as a technical measure (app/(marketing)/legal/dpa/page.tsx:82-88). Detecting a bulk export today would require database-side query logging, which is not enabled on Neon here.
findings.fix: Add the `data_access_audit` table and write path specified in design section 10: actor id, action, resource type, resource id, outcome, request id, hashed IP and timestamp — and never the PII value itself. Instrument the single choke point in lib/api/index.ts (withAuth) and lib/api/with-db-auth.ts (withDbAuth) plus the storage signed-URL endpoint.
findings.fix_notes: No read-access audit trail exists. The reconciliation_audit table exists but does not record sensitive reads.

findings.title: The privacy policy claims row-level security that the primary database does not have
findings.evidence: The privacy policy states: 'We use Supabase's row-level security to ensure that one landlord can never see another landlord's data.' The primary database is Neon and the migration header is explicit: 'No auth.users foreign keys - user_id is a plain uuid. Application code is responsible for scoping every query by the authenticated user's id' (db/migrations/001-core.sql:9-13). lib/api/with-db-auth.ts:14-15 repeats it: 'The handler must explicitly scope every query by userId - there's no RLS on Neon, so the application code carries that responsibility.' The RLS policies in supabase-setup/*.sql apply only to the legacy Supabase fallback path.
findings.impact: The published isolation guarantee does not describe the production architecture. Tenant isolation on Neon rests entirely on every query remembering `.eq("user_id", userId)`; one forgotten predicate is a cross-tenant breach and there is no database-level backstop — app/api/mpesa/c2b/validation/route.ts:75-80 is a live example of an unscoped query. The statement is the kind of sentence quoted verbatim in a breach notification, an enterprise security questionnaire, or a regulator's finding.
findings.fix: Two acceptable options: (a) immediate — correct the policy text to describe the actual architecture (application-layer scoping on Neon, RLS on the Supabase fallback); (b) hardening — put RLS on Neon using request.jwt.claim.sub with a per-transaction role setting. Recommend (a) now as a one-paragraph edit that removes a false statement, and (b) in the hardening cycle.
findings.fix_notes: The privacy policy still claims row-level security. This is a copy fix, and it needs the owner to decide what the platform actually promises. See audit/findings/features.json FEAT-016.

findings.title: The published sub-processor list names the wrong primary database
findings.evidence: The privacy policy states: 'Your data is stored in our Supabase (PostgreSQL) project, hosted on AWS.' The DPA sub-processor list states 'Supabase (PostgreSQL hosting) - primary database' and 'Amazon Web Services - backup storage (encrypted)'. The actual primary database is Neon (@neondatabase/serverless, lib/db/neon.ts:19) and backups go to Supabase Storage (lib/storage.ts:14), not to AWS.
findings.impact: Neon is a sub-processor that is not disclosed on the page customers sign, and its region is not disclosed either. Under Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 a processor must disclose its sub-processors; under GDPR Art. 28 the same. A customer performing a transfer-impact assessment from this list is working from incorrect facts, and the 'AWS' entry conceals that the primary datastore is a different vendor with a different region and a different breach history.
findings.fix: Add Neon and its region to the sub-processor list on the privacy page, the DPA page and app/(marketing)/sub-processors, and correct the backup-storage vendor. Cross-check app/(marketing)/help/page.tsx:68, which repeats the same claim.

findings.title: 'Backups are encrypted at rest' is not true of the application's own backup artefacts
findings.evidence: The privacy policy states 'Backups are encrypted at rest and in transit'; the security page states 'Daily encrypted backups, multi-region failover on the Agency tier.' The artefacts are plaintext JSON: uploaded with contentType application/json and no encryption (lib/storage.ts:36-40) and persisted inline as `payload: record.payload` in a jsonb column (lib/backup.ts:297). The backups bucket has no storage policy defined anywhere in supabase-setup/.
findings.impact: 'Encrypted at rest' is only true of the hosting provider's disk. The artefact itself is readable by anyone holding the service-role key, is downloadable by the account owner at any time, and is re-uploaded on every scheduled run. The claim materially overstates the control, and the backups bucket has an undefined privacy posture — public or private, with no policies.
findings.fix: Encrypt the backup payload with a dedicated key before persisting or uploading and define explicit policies for the backups bucket (design section 9); then the claim is accurate. Otherwise reword both pages to say 'infrastructure-level disk encryption at rest; application-level encryption of the tenant's personal data'.

findings.title: The security page advertises 'AES-256 at rest' and per-tenant keys that do not exist
findings.evidence: 'TLS 1.3 in transit. AES-256 at rest. Per-tenant encryption keys in our roadmap.' There is no application-layer encryption in the repository (CRYPTO-007) and no per-tenant key mechanism. The same page is the canonical description of the processor's technical and organisational measures, linked from the DPA at app/(marketing)/legal/dpa/page.tsx:82-88.
findings.impact: A security representation the code does not support, published to enterprise prospects and cited in a contractual document. If the design in this track is implemented the claim becomes true for the columns in the plan — but only for those columns, and the page still needs to distinguish infrastructure disk encryption from application field encryption.
findings.fix: Implement the design, then re-word precisely: which fields are field-encrypted, which are covered only by infrastructure encryption, and what the per-tenant key roadmap actually delivers.

findings.title: The DPA promises EU/Nairobi residency and 90-day post-termination deletion; neither exists
findings.evidence: 'Personal data is primarily stored in the EU (Frankfurt) and Kenya (Nairobi) regions ... Customers may request region locking on Agency and Enterprise plans.' and 'Within 90 days of subscription termination, PropDesk Africa will delete all personal data associated with the customer account, except where retention is mandated by law (e.g. financial records for 7 years).' There is no region-selection code anywhere, and no subscription-termination or cancellation handler that deletes data — app/api/subscription/** and app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts:26-45 only flip subscription status.
findings.impact: A contractual deletion SLA with nothing behind it, and a residency commitment that cannot be honoured. The gap compounds CRYPTO-012: even if a customer cancels and requests deletion, no code path would comply, so national IDs and M-Pesa records remain in Neon and — worse — in the 50 retained plaintext backups per user (CRYPTO-014).
findings.fix: Implement the termination purge by reusing the account-deletion routine from CRYPTO-012, and either implement region selection or reword the residency clause to describe the actual Neon region.

findings.title: PII is duplicated into columns and free-text fields outside any encryption plan
findings.evidence: `contacts` has `email text` and `phone text` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:327-341) and is a first-class table in BACKUP_TABLES (lib/system.ts:37). `managed_landlords` holds `contact_email` and `contact_phone` (supabase-setup/10-holy-grail.sql:180-181). `user_profiles` holds the landlord's own `phone` and `address` (db/migrations/001-core.sql:38-39). The lease-expiry scan interpolates the tenant's full name into notifications.title and notifications.message (db/migrations/002-support.sql:12-13, :35-46). Every entity has an unconstrained `notes` text column (db/migrations/001-core.sql:91, :111, :134, :161, :197) that landlords routinely use to paste national ID numbers.
findings.impact: An encryption plan that stops at tenants.national_id and tenants.phone leaves exactly the same data classes in clear text one table over — in contacts, in the notification feed, in the landlord's own profile, and in free text. The free-text notes columns are the hard case: they cannot be encrypted column-wise without destroying search and the UI, and they are the most likely place for a landlord to have pasted an ID number.
findings.fix: Extend the column plan to contacts.email, contacts.phone, managed_landlords.contact_email, managed_landlords.contact_phone and user_profiles.phone. For free text, use data minimisation plus a DLP scrubber on write (detect and redact Kenyan national ID and M-Pesa receipt patterns and route them into an encrypted side column) rather than blanket encryption — see design section 7.

findings.title: Emergency-contact (third-party) PII is written by the API but does not exist in the Neon schema
findings.evidence: The API whitelist accepts `emergency_contact_name` / `emergency_contact_phone` and inserts them (app/api/tenants/route.ts:67-68, app/api/tenants/[id]/route.ts:59-60), but the Neon `tenants` table (db/migrations/001-core.sql:76-94) has neither column — only the Supabase-path table does (supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:64-65).
findings.impact: Data-protection-wise: a third party's phone number (the emergency contact, who is neither the landlord nor the tenant) is collected and stored with no classification, no retention rule, and no mention in the privacy policy's 'what we collect' list (app/(marketing)/legal/privacy/page.tsx:31-38 covers only 'Account data' and 'Property data'). Operationally: on the Neon path these inserts fail on the unknown column, so the two database paths have diverged and any inventory reading only db/migrations/*.sql will miss real columns.
findings.fix: Add the two columns to a new db/migrations/003-*.sql with the data class PII (third party), give them the same treatment as contacts.phone, and add them to the privacy page's collection list. The design's inventory must cover both schema sources (db/migrations/*.sql and supabase-setup/*.sql).

findings.title: The C2B validation endpoint reads across every landlord's tenant rows with no tenant scoping
findings.evidence: isReasonableTransaction runs `select id from public.tenants where phone = ... or phone like ...` with no user_id filter, on a public unauthenticated endpoint (app/api/mpesa/c2b/validation/route.ts:32-35). The paybill owner is known (resolveOwnerByShortCode, app/api/mpesa/c2b/confirmation/route.ts:98-117) but is not applied here. The function then falls through to `return true` (:95-97, 'accept by default'), so the query is not even load-bearing for the accept/reject decision.
findings.impact: The endpoint reads the identity column of every tenant on the platform on every C2B payment attempt, with no tenant scoping, and leaks the answer through response timing. It is concrete proof that 'there is no RLS on Neon, so the application code carries that responsibility' (lib/api/with-db-auth.ts:14-15) is a live risk rather than a theoretical one, and it is the strongest single argument for putting RLS on Neon.
findings.fix: Scope the query to the paybill owner (`and t.user_id = ${ownerUserId}`) and, once phone is encrypted, look it up through the blind index (CRYPTO-002). If the 'accept by default' fallback is kept, the query can simply be deleted.
findings.fix_notes: app/api/mpesa/c2b/validation/route.ts still queries across every landlord tenant rows with no tenant scope. The fix is specified (blind-index lookup with an owner scope) but not implemented — it depends on the encryption wiring in CRYPTO-002.

findings.title: The service-role key is used in user-facing write paths, disabling the storage policies
findings.evidence: The photo upload route creates a service-role client and uses it for the upload; the M-Pesa callback and the Stripe webhook do the same for their writes. The service-role key bypasses every RLS and storage policy — that is its purpose (lib/supabase/service.ts:5-13).
findings.impact: The service-role key is the platform's real master credential: it can read and write every table and every bucket for every landlord, including the documents bucket the storage policies were supposed to guard. The policies at supabase-setup/01-create-tables.sql:336-351 therefore protect only the paths that deliberately avoid the service role. Any code path that helpfully upgrades to the service key silently voids the isolation model — which is exactly what happened to property photos (CRYPTO-006).
findings.fix: Restrict service-role usage to the genuinely public callbacks (M-Pesa C2B validation/confirmation, Stripe webhook, backup cron) and to the storage signed-URL helper; use the user-scoped client everywhere else, including uploads. Record the key in the key-management runbook with its rotation procedure, and never expose it in a NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable.

findings.title: The dashboard reads sensitive columns directly from the browser, bypassing the server
findings.evidence: These are 'use client' components that build the browser Supabase client (lib/supabase/client.ts:11-20) and read the tables straight from PostgREST: `const supabase = createClient()` then `supabase.from("tenants").select(`*, properties (id, name, address, rent_amount, monthly_rent)`)` (app/dashboard/tenants/[id]/page.tsx:29-34). `select("*")` returns national_id and phone in clear text to the browser. Every write goes through the server (components/tenant-form.tsx:85 -> apiFetch("/api/tenants")), so the asymmetry is read-side only.
findings.impact: Two consequences. (1) Security: the entire sensitive-column read surface is reachable from the browser with the anon key that ships in the client bundle, with no server mediation, no audit trail and no rate limit — only the Supabase-path RLS policies stand in the way, and the Neon path has no RLS at all (CRYPTO-016). (2) It is a hard blocker for application-layer encryption: the browser cannot decrypt a `v1:...` envelope because the key must never be sent to the client, so until these reads are proxied through the server, encrypting tenants.national_id makes the tenant detail page render `v1:IvTagCt...` instead of the ID number.
findings.fix: Add server routes (or convert the pages to server components) that read the sensitive tables and decrypt server-side, and change the client components to call them. Files to convert: app/dashboard/tenants/**, app/dashboard/properties/[id]/**, app/dashboard/contacts/**, app/dashboard/documents/**, app/dashboard/paybill/**, app/dashboard/reconciliation/**. This is Phase 0 of audit/design/encryption-design.md section 11.
findings.fix_notes: The dashboard still reads sensitive columns from the browser. The encryption deliverable designates this as PHASE 0, blocking: the exact list of pages is in audit/deliverable-encryption-core.md section 5.0 and HARDENING_RUNBOOK.md section 4.2.
